brief: JPMorgan and Goldman have converged on August 2027 as when Treasury must start raising coupon auction sizes, both having delayed their prior calls (Goldman from May). The driver is widening deficits (FY26 $1.992T, JPMorgan sees FY27 at $2.06T/6.1% GDP, FY28 $2.25T) producing a roughly $1.6T FY27-28 funding gap as COVID-era note maturities crowd the calendar. The debt ceiling, binding around February 2027, buys time via negative net bill issuance through Q2, which is why August and not sooner. The banks split sharply on who absorbs the resulting bill flood: JPMorgan says traditional buyers (money funds, foreign officials, stablecoins) are tapped out and halves its Fed bill-purchase forecast to $180bn, since Warsh's balance-sheet task force could end even that reinvestment; Goldman expects the Fed to resume reserve-management purchases, absorbing roughly half a trillion. Early evidence (the New York Fed's schedule showing a fourth month with no reserve-management purchases) favors JPMorgan's read. Both keep long-end auction sizes unchanged, against Citi's call for cuts. JPMorgan also flags a possible new 1-year SOFR floating-rate note in 2027.
